rationale: A central computer as the brain, nerves and heart of an asteroid station points toward whole-station control, but Skylab's computer only handled attitude and pointing, not life support.
The machine reads information straight from a mind, but the Kyoto work only rebuilt crude 10x10 images a subject was looking at, a much narrower function.
Matching measured crystal properties against stored memory banks resembles database lookup, but Dialog searched bibliographic records by keyword, not physical-property identification.
A speaking robot that dismisses its subject shows speech only; nothing in the line shows understanding of typed English like ELIZA's pattern matching.
Robot ears that turn toward a commanding voice anticipate machines obeying speech, but the line gives no recognition mechanism and Apricot was a 1984 word-list recognizer.
A machine run by mental impulses matches the aim of thought-controlled devices, but the quote only requests one and Johnny Ray's implant moved a cursor by recorded neural signals.
Interrogation data taped into central computers that notify police resembles a networked records system, but NCIC was a lookup database for wanted persons, not integration of interrogation data.
A robot carrying its creator's mind as an extension of his intelligence is not a physical double; Lincoln's animatronic was a lookalike figure with scripted speech.
Gates that recognize a person and open match face-based access control in function, but the quote gives no mechanism and ZN-Face used camera image matching.
A computer naming an object as a gun from stored data is a loose retrieval-by-matching idea, far from Dialog's keyword search of document databases.
Speaking into an order box that returns a card is a voice-driven fetch of records, close to voice command, though recognition is not described and Apricot was a small PC feature.
Deliberately feeding a machine a problem to drive it insane is sabotage of a computer, but the 1967 APL network penetration was unauthorized access, not paradox attack.
The line only says a robot shares Central Intelligence's physics beliefs; nothing here shows one computer directing many robots as Kiva fulfilment did.
Speaking the date into a laboratory machine's microphone anticipates voice input to a computer, but the line shows no recognition or command execution.
A sensipsych training device beside books hints at machine-aided learning, but the line gives no lessons, testing or grading as in PLATO.
Testing a system by fighting duels points at interactive simulated combat, but nothing in the line shows many people sharing a networked world like MUD1.
A ring token triggering a photo-electronic door mechanism matches a machine-read access token, though by light rather than punched holes and with no identity encoded.
Power machinery made completely automatic and needing only a handful of attendants matches a lights-out plant in function, but without robots building robots or the stated mechanism.
Checking moon gravity and distance on an onboard computer to decide a maneuver matches shipboard orbital computation in function, but the 1965 case involved burn calculation by the computer.
A plastic chip bearing a pressed fingerprint for boarding resembles an identity token verified by machine, but here it is a record checked by a clerk, not read automatically.
Speaking a memo into a voicewrite is dictation by machine, though the line does not show transcription, and Dragon Dictate took discrete words.
Going wherever home is evokes a personalized created world, but the line gives no sensory display or computer mechanism like the Virtuality 1000SU.
A door microphone that follows a person and a hi-fi choosing tapes suggest responsive appliances, but ECHO IV was a home computer controlling household routines.
A three-dimensional space model with new dots added is a volumetric map, but the Multiplex hologram was a viewable-around cylinder image, not a live planning model.
Reading enemy plans from brains with an educator machine points at extracting mental content, but the real work only decoded viewed images.
A state records system telling a cooker to feed a person more is networked appliance control, but ECHO IV was a single household computer, not a state system.
An electronic brain that plays games and has military use is only a sketch; SAGE was an air-defence tracking system, not game-playing.
A selector with thirty-two kinds of automatic controls suggests station-wide automation, but Skylab's computer only handled attitude and pointing.
Punching keys on computers that do astral mathematics is shipboard navigation computation in function, but no mechanism or maneuvering is shown.
An electronic cross-index delivering newspaper files is an indexing system, but nothing in the quote mentions speech or voice commands.
A machine matching a photograph to a complete file in seconds matches fast record retrieval, though Dialog retrieved text citations by keyword, not images.
A microscopic electronic brain is about miniature intelligence; Stoddart's rotaxane shuttle was a molecular mechanical switch, a different thing.
A central information institution that answers any question resembles broad lookup, but it relies on human or robot operators, unlike Dialog's database query.
A mechanical man that commits suicide hints at a humanoid robot, but the line shows no walking, speaking or object handling like Elektro.
Exact translation of oral sound into text anticipates speech-to-text dictation, but no mechanism is given and Dragon Dictate in 1990 handled discrete words.
A house that announces it supplies wants and feeds you suggests a service-providing home, but ECHO IV merely ran household chores through a computer.
Robots keeping solved problems stored for repetition resembles learning from experience, but SNARC learned a maze by reinforcement rather than storing solutions.
A computer miscalculating burn mass for a lunar rocket points at onboard maneuver calculation, but the quote is a failure and the 1965 case was a working orbital adjustment.
A table map showing the red circles of air-cities matches a live situation display of tracked objects, though SAGE used computer-driven radar consoles, not a mounted map.
A mechanical cortex of ninety billion electronic cells echoes neuron-like units, but the line says nothing of learning and LeNet was a trained recognizer of digits.
A door rising at a woman's voice is a voice-operated door in function, but the quote shows no recognition mechanism; Apricot was a PC word recognizer.
The quote only describes a man's expression changing; it says nothing of fingerprints, so it does not match AFIS research.
Sleeping in nutrient baths in personal dream worlds anticipates being fed a lived world, but nothing here describes computer-generated senses like the arcade systems.
A computer noting a crime upswing is crime-trend analysis, but NCIC was a lookup database of wanted persons and stolen property, not analysis.
An electronic brain that plays games is not shown to play chess, and the Fidelity Chess Challenger was a consumer chess machine.
A subconscious analysis test is about psychological assessment; UCSF decoded attempted speech from cortical signals into text, which is not shown.
A perfect illusion touching all senses matches immersive VR in function, but there is no mechanism and the Virtuality 1000SU was a headset system.
Collars delivering machine answers as mental impulses is brain input from computers, whereas the Johnny Ray implant sent brain signals out to move a cursor.
Thoughts linked to hidden machinery in a metal square points to mind-machine coupling, but the quote offers no mechanism or controlled device.
Cybernetically controlled stations needing no human matches a self-running plant, but without the robot-built products and 30-day lights-out runs of Fanuc.
A cybernetic brain controlling quality regulators in all factories at once matches automated plant control, but nothing shows no human workers or robots making robots.
Androids needing guidance and some means of command only imply a controller; the quote is inference, not a central computer coordinating robots like Kiva.
Gadgets that detect thought-waves point loosely at brain-signal sensing, but no thought content is read as in the Kyoto reconstruction.
Humans feeding data to machines whose answers a coordinator humanizes suggests a computer-assisted team, but SAGE linked radar sites to computers.
Sliding fingers over a sparkling panel to enter text matches touch-panel input, though the PLATO IV panel was an infrared grid for answering questions.
A giant computer behind a private intelligence outfit that agencies rely on is a big answering machine, but the quote shows no natural-language questions like START.
Central Intelligence being the creator of perfect plans says nothing about directing robots; it is not the Kiva coordination.
A keyboard to control humanlike servants and follow their courses is remote command, but the Goertz manipulator was a master-slave device with sensory feedback.
A thumbhole opening a door suggests thumb-based access, but nothing says the thumb print is matched by machine as in Wegstein's fingerprint models.
A robot attuned to thought waves obeys a person, a loose neural-control idea, but nothing here decodes particular thoughts or images.
A chamber where light, gas and music make wishes take form matches multisensory immersion, but without a computer-generated display like the Virtuality 1000SU.
Thought images thrown on a screen anticipate showing mental content, but UCSF decoded spoken sentences into text, not images.
Telling the ship what he wants to do anticipates spoken navigation commands, but Apricot recognized a small word list for software, not piloting.
Computing the motions of thousands of stars to a quarter-mile is heavy shipboard calculation, but the 1965 case was orbital maneuvering on a crewed capsule.
Radioactive pyramidal cells that overheat are an imaginary device with no resemblance to LeNet digit recognition.
Thousands of ships tied by robot controls to act in coordination match one controller directing many machines, though the Kiva system moved warehouse carts.
A concealed robot brain able to control a car anticipates vehicle autonomy, but the line gives no sensing and Tsukuba's car used cameras on street markings.
Communication between a girl and a computer by ESP is telepathy, not navigation computing, so it does not match the onboard computer milestone.
A hidden camera reading a raised palm to log workers is biometric identification, not a machine-read card, so it loosely matches VALI-DINE.
Feeding space coordinates to a shipboard computer to find the nearest stars is star lookup, while the 1965 milestone was computing orbital maneuvers.
A mechanical voice stating a rule to a robot shows machine speech, but the quote does not show how it is produced, while the 1976 devices used synthesis.
Analyzing filmed brain-wave patterns into a live bedside image is brain monitoring, not MYCIN's rule-based diagnosis of infections.
A shipboard Brain feeding out tape is a calculating machine for colonization data, not an orbital guidance computer.
A keyless machine recording dictation as a waveform on paper replaces a secretary, but it is not text, unlike Dragon Dictate.
Fingerprint and retinal pattern checks match retina scanning for identity, though the quote gives little mechanism and EyeDentify was a retinal scanner product.
A circular graph that pulses on a control table points toward a tracking display, but SAGE consoles showed computer-processed radar tracks.
An oracle that answers any question promptly and completely matches question-answering, though without mechanism, whereas START answered English questions from a knowledge base.
A computer reporting radio messages between a man and his ship is signal interception, but ECHELON screened satellite traffic by keyword at scale.
Machines behind walls that prepare meals and select music describe a service home, but ECHO IV controlled household routines through a computer.
Machines that cannot integrate an anomalous datum is a story about failing prediction, not SAGE air-defence tracking.
A thought-helmet entering an alien's brain is about reading minds with hardware, but no decoded image or data is shown as in the Kyoto reconstruction.
An animated three-dimensional star map on a wall suggests volumetric display, but the Multiplex hologram was a cylinder-viewed film, not an animated map.
A legal and policy information bank queried by unit number is a database, but START answered open natural-language questions.
An implant triggered by nerve signals gives a device input, whereas the cochlear implant delivered sound by stimulating the nerve.
A machine with electrodes that voices a person's thoughts is closer to Chang and Makin's speech decoding than ATR's images, but the real systems read attempted speech.
A sensipsych machine's vivid visions teaching skills hints at simulation-based training, but the quote gives no computer-generated senses as in Virtuality 1000SU.
An arrow into a robot's braincase says nothing about a computer that coordinates robots.
Ship computers with problem-solving circuits that time a braking burn match onboard computation of engine burns, though only loosely described.
Recorded music tuned to his mood from concealed amplifiers is responsive entertainment, narrow next to ECHO IV's home computer.
A repair robot reprogrammed to build ever smaller circuits touches on miniaturization, but integrated circuits were solid-state chips.
A machine building factories and robot workers matches robots making robots, but the quote relies on telekinesis, not Fanuc's lights-out plant.
Humanlike mechanoids organized in ranks says nothing of a central computer coordinating robots as in Kiva.
A large computer used as an integrator by the sciences suggests a general problem-answering machine, but the quote lacks language answers like START.
A lock opened by timed light pulses is an access mechanism, but it resembles a combination, not an identity-encoded card.
A brain wired by multiplex cable to a typewriter communicates by output, matching a direct interface, though the real implant moved a cursor.
Calculators that plot a survey route in advance suggest course planning, but the 1965 milestone was an onboard computer performing orbital maneuvers.
A voice-cued setter that records memos on a spoken password matches voice command in function, though it differs in being wearable.
Robots acting as repositories of knowledge teaching children point at machine instruction, but PLATO I presented lessons and graded answers.
Vocowriters as equipment for people matches machines turning speech into text, but the quote gives no function beyond the name.
Turning thought into visible expression for all to read hints at thought display, but UCSF decoded spoken sentences into text from cortical signals.
Electronic computers that direct the speed of fast ships match onboard computer control, though no calculation is described.
Putting figures into a spaceship computer is a minimal reference to onboard computation, with no maneuver or steering shown.
Barking a command into an order box matches voice command, though the quote says nothing of recognition or the kind of machine.
A tiny identoflake in a bracelet flashed onto screens is an identity token read by machine, but optical rather than a punched card.
Giant electronic computers do the mathematics of orbital insertion, matching the heavy computation of NORC for ballistics, though the use differs.
Automated customs scanners and paper-checkers point at machine reading of documents, but the quote does not show reading characters as in postal sorting.
A helmet acting as a receiver that draws mental content out without sending current is a passive reading idea, but no content is decoded like the Kyoto reconstruction.
A semantic integrator compiling battle reports for a fleet admiral suggests data fusion, whereas SAGE tracked aircraft for air defence.
A scanner turning book pages and sending text to distant analysts is scanning, but the quote does not show characters turned into data as in mail sorting.
A triggered electronic key that opens airlocks is an access device, but the quote gives no encoded identity as on a VALI-DINE card.
The quote is only a character's inward curse, with no retinal scanning, so it does not match EyeDentify.
A scanner that recognizes fingerprints and opens the door matches automated fingerprint recognition, though Wegstein's work was analysis of prints, not door control.
Machines that write complete stories match automatic composition of text, but FoG generated weather forecasts from data rather than fiction.
Programmed toy dogs that cannot bite match a robot pet, but Gaylord was a leash-steered toy rather than a circuit-run animal.
Tube blocks holding plots and dialogue that generate fiction match automatic writing from stored material, but FoG produced forecasts, not fiction.
A magnetically encoded tab clipped from a dashboard is a machine-read vehicle record, but VALI-DINE cards identified people for access.
A tri-dim chart across a room is a volumetric display of positions, but the Multiplex hologram was a film cylinder.
A naturally formed helium brain with neuron-like circuits is a story creature, not a computer trained for digit recognition.
Buttons that unlock when pressed in chorded patterns is a panel input method, but not touch or gesture sensing as on PLATO IV.
A robot brain with a dowsing sense for water is not Audrey's spoken-digit hearing, so no sense is anticipated.
A cabinet of drawers from which verse imagery is picked is a mechanized aid to poetry, but FoG generated text from data.
A robot's speaker negotiating terms shows machine speech, but a typed English pattern-matching conversation like ELIZA is not shown.
Machine sifting of wreckage for registration plates is automated reading, but the quote does not describe reading characters by optical means.
A black fuzzy robot cat that hunts mice is an animal robot, though Gaylord was a leash-steered toy dog.
An electronic astrogator on rockets using coded impulses is an onboard computer for navigation, but the 1965 case concerned orbital maneuvers on a crewed capsule.
A means of reproducing every sensation of living matches immersive VR in function, but there is no mechanism, whereas Virtuality 1000SU used a headset.
A door that announces visitors is speech output, not recognition, so it only loosely resembles Apricot's voice commands.
Identification tabs carrying a psychometric number are encoded tokens read by scanners, but VALI-DINE used punched holes to open doors.
A canned voice interrogating a visitor matches machine speech output, but the line does not show how it is synthesized, as in the Kurzweil machine.
Running a multi-beacon problem through the navigator is shipboard course computation, but not the orbital maneuvering of 1965.
A hypnosis beam that reads innermost thought is a remote mind reader, but the Kyoto work reconstructed viewed images using brain signals.
Lights in the brain that blot vision suggest a computer feeding images in, whereas the cursor-control milestone read brain signals out.
A referral to a big system computer implies linked machines, but the quote does not show terminals on communication lines as in SAGE.
A records unit that identifies a girl fitting stated requirements matches computer matchmaking, but the 1964 service compared questionnaires.
A machine that detects when a mind is being read is a counter-telepathy detector, not a reader of thoughts.
Comptometers plotting warp paths and holding the ship at critical speeds are onboard calculators steering a vessel, though the 1965 computer did orbital burns.
Half-inch micro-robots with electron vision are small robots, not molecular machines like the rotaxane shuttle.
Taking a retina pattern from a person for identification matches retina scanning, though here it is photographed and sent to a records office.
A figure whose word-repeater reacts to sounds is a speech-triggered device, but it only sways to sounds, with no recognition of words.
A house run by an electronic brain suggests an automated home, but the quote names no function like ECHO IV's household routines.
A fully automated assembly line matches a self-operating factory, but making android bodies differs from Fanuc's robots building robots.
A stereographic device showing a captive's thoughts as moving pictures anticipates thought display, but UCSF decoded text, not 3D images.
Thinking a world into being hints at brain-driven control, but the Johnny Ray implant moved a cursor and nothing here shows signals measured.
A chess game worked out by masters with high-speed computers involves computers in chess, but not machines that play, unlike the Chess Challenger.
A book-screen to read from is an electronic book display, but the Data Discman played books from mini-CD.
A brain-modelled giant computer that solves problems at superhuman speed echoes neural designs, but the quote names no neurons or learning.
Machinery that opens only to one person's characteristic motions is a personal access control, but VALI-DINE read punched cards.
A Menograph recording thoughts onto tape in place of pen and pencil matches thought-to-text in function, with no mechanism shown, unlike UCSF's decoding.
A subject thrust into a situation experienced as fully real is immersive simulation, but the line gives no equipment like the Virtuality 1000SU.
Transparent index cards with a last-reported-location ticket track people by a manual file, not a device reporting position like NIMCOS.
